clue.text: Descriptive of heels, or of toes, maltreated

indicators.note: letters that are maltreated are knocked about and rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone describes heels and toes that have been badly treated by tight shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maltreated' rearranges OR OF TOES. Heels here are the walker's own, worn sore by walking.
explanation.definitionFit: Walkers' heels that ache after a long tramp are described as tender in this way.

clue.text: Neat hospital worker

explanation.surface: A tidy person who works in a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat means tidy and well arranged; a hospital attendant who does non-medical tasks has the same title.

clue.text: To us, holding a lot of foreign money is worrying

indicators.note: the words to us hold something inside them, as a container clasps its contents

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a lot of a word, but not all, means its final letter is dropped

parts.note: the rouble is the currency of Russia

explanation.surface: Someone frets that we are being lumbered with a pile of foreign cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts ROUBL (the Russian rouble without its last letter, from 'a lot of') inside TO US.
explanation.definitionFit: Something troublous is full of disturbance, so it causes anxiety; an old literary synonym.

clue.text: Jogger's seen headless horseman

indicators.note: without its head means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: to jog someone is to jostle or nudge them, so a jogger is a jostler

explanation.surface: A headless horseman is spotted by someone out jogging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jogger' suggests a runner, but here it is one who jogs elbows. 'headless' removes the first letter of JOSTLER.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostler looked after the horses at an inn, a stableman by trade.

clue.text: Author of "Eagles on the China Road'

parts.note: an erne is a sea eagle, a crossword favourite
taken as written
Ming was a Chinese dynasty, standing for China
a way is a road

explanation.surface: It looks like the title of a book about birds of prey in the Far East.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks pretend this is a real title; the pieces simply sit side by side, with 'on' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Hemingway was the American novelist of The Old Man and the Sea, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Latitude for subject imprisoning king

indicators.note: the word for subject locks the king up inside it, holding him captive

parts.note: a topic is a subject of discussion
R is short for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A ruler is jailed for the sake of the country's freedom.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropics of Cancer and Capricorn are parallels of latitude, lines circling the globe.

clue.text: Won by the team that retires

definitions.text: Won by the team that retires

parts.words: Won by the team that retires
parts.note: the contest is won by the side that keeps stepping backwards, hauling the rope its way

explanation.surface: A paradox: the team that withdraws comes out on top.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rope-pulling contest the winners move backwards, dragging opponents over the line.

clue.text: One fine day, he scored it

definitions.text: One fine day, he scored it

parts.words: One fine day, he scored it
parts.note: One Fine Day is the English title of a famous soprano aria, and scoring it means composing its music

explanation.surface: Someone, one sunny day, notched up a goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Un bel di', One Fine Day, is Butterfly's aria from Madama Butterfly; 'scored' means set to music, not netted a goal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian opera composer wrote Madama Butterfly, which contains the aria Un bel di.

clue.text: Follow good example, in measure against piracy

explanation.surface: Imitating a worthy model is cast as a defence against pirates.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is read as two words: copy right, imitate correctly. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To copy right is to imitate correctly; the legal protection of authors stops their work being pirated.

clue.text: Skilful, and have right continental style

parts.note: in French, a is the verb form meaning has
droit is French for right

explanation.surface: Being clever is likened to having a European flair for being correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'continental style' tells the solver the pieces are French; it is a pointer, not an operation.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit means dexterous and clever with the hands or mind.

clue.text: Drink that goes to one's head

definitions.text: Drink that goes to one's head

parts.words: Drink that goes to one's head
parts.note: a bedtime drink, but also the cap worn on the head in bed

explanation.surface: A strong drink that makes someone tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedtime alcoholic drink shares its name with the cap once worn to bed.

clue.text: State without colour bar sends mixture

indicators.note: a mixture is a jumble, so the letters before it are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: A colour bar is being enforced in a state, apparently producing a mix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without colour bar' reads as about segregation, but the definition ends at 'colour'; 'mixture' rearranges BAR SENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dullness is the condition of lacking bright colour or interest.

clue.text: See back of Matilda — leaves like this?

indicators.note: back means the little word of is turned to read the other way

parts.note: Belloc's cautionary tale Matilda told such dreadful lies that she was burned to death

explanation.surface: Someone is told to look at the end of a story about Matilda.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is a link. Matilda is the girl in Hilaire Belloc's verse who 'told such dreadful lies'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to plant leaves, as in a leaf-applied feed.

clue.text: Lay lord?

parts.note: a nobleman who wrote lays, that is narrative poems, rather than a lord of the laity

explanation.surface: A peer who is not a churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romantic poet was the sixth Baron of his line and wrote long verse tales.

clue.text: South Sea transport?

parts.note: the South Sea Bubble was an 18th-century financial collapse, so its vehicle would be named after it

explanation.surface: A ship in the Pacific.
explanation.walkthrough: The South Sea Bubble was a famous British share-price crash of 1720.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny domed three-wheeler of the 1950s took its name from a bubble, playing on the crash.

clue.text: Object about hasty punishment

indicators.note: the word for object goes around the other piece, standing about it

parts.note: a thing is an object
rash means hasty

explanation.surface: Someone objects to a punishment handed out too quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb of protest but is the noun THING.
explanation.definitionFit: A beating is a punishment, as a heavy flogging.

clue.text: Chance puts Herbert in danger

indicators.note: Herbert is set in the word for danger

parts.note: hazard means danger
APH were the initials A. P. Herbert signed his humorous writing with

explanation.surface: Fate puts a man named Herbert in peril.
explanation.walkthrough: A. P. Herbert was a British humorist and MP who signed himself APH. 'puts' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word once meant mere luck or accident, as in 'at haphazard'.

clue.text: In "dicey" situation the lady's angelic

indicators.note: the lady is placed in the dicey word

parts.note: dice are cubes, so dicey is taken as cube-shaped
the lady's belongings are hers, giving her

explanation.surface: In a risky situation a woman is nonetheless saintly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dicey' seems to mean risky; read literally, it is shaped like dice. 'situation' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A cherub is a childlike angel, so the adjective means sweet and innocent like one.

clue.text: Curse when sheep and lamb go astray

indicators.note: when the animals go astray their letters wander out of order

explanation.surface: A farmer swears when the flock wanders off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'go astray' rearranges SHEEP and LAMB; 'and' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: To blaspheme is to speak profanely, to swear.

clue.text: Difficult as the RAF's Star trek?

definitions.text: Difficult as the RAF's Star trek?

parts.words: Difficult as the RAF's Star trek?
parts.note: the Royal Air Force motto is Per ardua ad astra, through hardships to the stars

explanation.surface: A space voyage is as hard as an air force mission.
explanation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force; its Latin motto means 'through adversity to the stars'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means laborious, from the same Latin root as the motto's hardships.

clue.text: Jack's mackerel bait

explanation.surface: Someone's bait for catching mackerel.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Sprat of the nursery rhyme 'could eat no fat'; 'a sprat to catch a mackerel' is a proverb.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme Jack's surname is a small fish, the proverbial small bait risked for a bigger catch.

clue.text: Windy that trouble will arise in time

indicators.note: the trouble word goes in the time word

parts.note: an aeon is a vast stretch of time

indicators.note: in a down answer, arising means the word reads from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: Someone predicts that a gust of trouble will blow up eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will arise' turns AIL to LIA, set in AEON.
explanation.definitionFit: Aeolus was the Greek keeper of the winds, so the adjective means produced by the wind.

clue.text: Note rascal making this sort of speech in Ireland

definitions.text: this sort of speech in Ireland

parts.note: B is a musical note
a rogue is a rascal

explanation.surface: Someone notes a rascal speaking like an Irishman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish brogue is a strong regional accent.

clue.text: Helpful steps for one learning arithmetic?

definitions.text: Helpful steps for one learning arithmetic?

parts.words: Helpful steps for one learning arithmetic?
parts.note: read as a boy who is learning to add, plus a set of rungs to climb

explanation.surface: Advice on stages for a child mastering sums.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as LAD + ADDER: a youngster who adds.
explanation.definitionFit: Rungs that help someone climb, and also a boy who sums.

clue.text: His relations get a hearing

parts.note: relations are things related, i.e. stories told, not relatives

explanation.surface: A man's relatives are given a chance to speak in court.
explanation.definitionFit: A storyteller recounts tales, which listeners then hear.

clue.text: Wielded by belligerent and irate oarsman

parts.note: cross means angry
bow is the rower nearest the front of a boat

explanation.surface: An angry, warlike rower brandishes something.
explanation.walkthrough: In rowing, the bow is the oarsman seated nearest the boat's front.
explanation.definitionFit: The mechanical bow is a weapon a fighter carries.

clue.text: Free from interminable gastric disorder

indicators.note: the remaining letters are put into disorder, rearranged
without an end, so the final letter is cut off

explanation.surface: A promise of relief from a never-ending stomach complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'interminable' drops the C of GASTRIC; 'disorder' rearranges GASTRI. 'from' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin-derived word means without charge.

clue.text: Like country with Red in charge

parts.note: rust is a reddish-brown colour

explanation.surface: A country is compared to one run by communists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red' suggests a communist; here it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustic means rural, belonging to the countryside.

clue.text: Being productive in firm? Certainly not

explanation.surface: Someone questions whether a company is profitable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a company; it is the adjective, and something not firm gives way. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Land that produces crops gives a harvest; something soft and pliant gives way, the opposite of firm.
